subject: Business
title: Hyperinflation in Weimar Germany
description: A 60-second lesson on Hyperinflation in Weimar Germany.

hook.text: In 1923, a loaf of bread in Berlin cost 200 billion marks. Workers carried wages in wheelbarrows.

buildup.text: After World War I, Germany owed massive reparations. The government printed money to pay debts.

discovery.text: Prices doubled every few days. People spent money the instant they received it because waiting meant it was worthless.

twist.text: The middle class was wiped out. Savings became worthless overnight. Social trust collapsed.

climax.text: Stability returned only when Germany introduced a new currency backed by land and mortgages — the Rentenmark.

punchline.text: Print enough money and money becomes meaningless.

quiz.question: What caused Weimar Germany's hyperinflation?
options: The government printed massive amounts of money to pay war reparations
A gold shortage caused prices to rise
Foreign banks manipulated the exchange rate

details.summary: Weimar Germany experienced catastrophic hyperinflation in 1923 when the mark lost virtually all value, reaching prices of trillions of marks for basic goods. The government printed money to pay war reparations, destroying savings and destabilizing society profoundly.
details.whyItMatters: Weimar hyperinflation is the most studied example of what happens when monetary policy fails completely. It demonstrates that money is only as stable as the institutions managing it and that inflation can spiral beyond all control.
takeaways: Prices doubled every few days at the peak of Weimar hyperinflation in 1923
Printing money to pay war debts triggered the inflationary spiral
The economic devastation contributed to political extremism and instability

faq.question: How extreme did Weimar hyperinflation actually get?
faq.answer: At its peak in November 1923, prices doubled every three to four days. A loaf of bread cost 200 billion marks. Workers were paid twice daily and rushed to spend wages before they lost value. People used wheelbarrows of cash to buy groceries.

faq.question: How was Weimar hyperinflation eventually stopped?
faq.answer: Germany introduced the Rentenmark in November 1923, backed by land and industrial assets rather than gold. The government committed to strict fiscal discipline and limited money printing. Confidence returned quickly and within months prices stabilized completely.
